News.title: Burned body of glam TikTok star, 29, is found in among grapevines at vineyard by farmer as murder probe launched
News.content:
TRAGIC FIND Burned body of glam TikTok star, 29, is found in among grapevines at vineyard by farmer as murder probe launched

A TIKTOK star with over 250,000 followers was found dead in a vineyard in France after disappearing.

The naked and partially burned body of Sonia Bellina, 29, was dumped in between grapevines in a remote rural area in Saint-Gilles, France.



A farmer stumbled upon her remains on August 12, 48 hours after she was reported missing.

Around 40 police officers were deployed to the scene and the area was quickly cordoned off.



Investigators have since ruled out accidental death due to the nature of the crime scene, and the case is now being treated as a suspected premeditated murder.

DNA tests have since confirmed the victim was the young woman, it was reported. The autopsy has been scheduled for this Thursday.



Few details have been released about the influencer’s last moments and her death as officers continue to scour the scene in Saint-Gilles.

Sonia’s sister spoke extensively about her disappearance in a livestream on TikTok.

She revealed that Sonia had gone out one evening and never returned.

She also mentioned physical items that, according to her, matched the body that was found – breast implants and a ring, Le Figaro reported.



Sonia was reportedly rumoured to have met a man the night before she went missing, but this has not been confirmed by police.

Her family released a statement earlier this week, addressing numerous derogatory comments published on social media about her appearance.

Mourad Battikh, the lawyer representing the victim’s family, said they are “going through an extremely violent ordeal.”



He further denounced the spread of “rumours, speculation, outrageous remarks, and accusations.”

“[This] adds to the unnecessary suffering to that of loved ones,” he said, also adding that it is likely to hinder the investigation.

Sonia’s social media career took off in 2020 and she remained highly active online until 2025, when her posts began to tail off.

News.title: Throwing good money after bad won’t solve the migrant problem… PM must implement a proper deterrent scheme
News.content:
French farce

BRITAIN can’t keep writing cheques to France and hoping the small boats crisis will somehow go away.

The solution is in our own hands — and it’s staring us in the face like the White Cliffs of Dover on a clear day.



Ministers must stop making the UK a major draw with generous benefits, free healthcare and access to cash-in-hand jobs on the black market.

French mayor Xavier Bertrand hit the nail on the head by saying that failure to enforce our own rules had made us a “permanent attraction” for asylum cheats.



But he wants British taxpayers to cough up even more money to mount beach patrols in Northern France.

We have already signed away £1billion, only for more than 14,500 illegal migrants to land on our shores this year alone.

Throwing good money after bad won’t solve the problem.

Andy Burnham must take tough action against rogue employers and implement a proper deterrent like the Rwanda scheme.

British taxpayers should not be expected to fund failure indefinitely.

Nice one Kemi

A RELIABLE power system should focus on keeping the lights on and the bills down — not a virtue-signalling race to hit Net Zero at any cost.



That’s why Kemi Badenoch is on to a winner with her plan to bring common sense to energy policy.

The Tory leader says a mix of nuclear, gas and renewable energy would save families £540 a year and still be 80 per cent clean.

That’s a huge gain.

With nearly 100,000 payroll jobs vanishing over the past year and wages stagnating, it’s hard to understand why the PM is stalling on giving the go-ahead to drill for North Sea oil and gas.

Even green campaigners, such as Labour donor Dale Vince, are waking up to the undeniable reality:



Cheaper, reliable, home-grown energy means lower bills and more jobs.

Royal courage

THE King and Queen have shown unyielding courage in the way they have faced cancer with dignity and honesty.

Charles has been an inspiration, opening up about his own diagnosis to smash the taboo and save lives.

His decision to go public led a 50 per cent increase in the number of people seeking guidance over their own symptoms.

Camilla has supported her husband while championing others facing the same cruel condition.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

She made the heart-wrenching decision to visit a cancer charity while harbouring the secret of her husband’s own diagnosis.

If their hard work and dedication has made just one person feel less frightened and alone, it will have achieved something truly worthwhile.

News.title: Brit dad, 41, died on holiday in Majorca with daughter after going on late night walk then plunging from 15ft wall
News.content:
TRAGIC END Brit dad, 41, died on holiday in Majorca with daughter after going on late night walk then plunging from 15ft wall

A BRIT dad tragically died on holiday in Majorca while taking a late night walk and falling from a 15ft cliff, an inquest heard.

Ben Clark, 41, died instantly after he fell into a rocky area in Cala Agulla in the early hours of the morning on June 26 last year.



The dad, who lived in Andover, Hampshire, was holidaying with his daughter, Kaci Fraya, for the first time, which he was “really excited” about.

Winchester Coroner’s Court heard on Tuesday that the pair had become friends with another British woman and her aunt who they socialised around the pool with on their trip.



Area coroner Jason Pegg said the evidence showed there was clearly “some attraction” between Ben and the woman, Nicky Foers.

They decided to go for a walk together down to the beach at around 11.30pm that evening.

The coroner said it seems “slightly unclear” what caused Ben to fall from the cliff but believed alcohol probably contributed to him losing his footing.

Mr Pegg said: “All of you, particularly your dad, had consumed alcohol.



“He was not completely staggering around and out of it, but [had been] drinking nonetheless.

“There came a time on that cliff top where your dad was looking out to sea, Ms Foers looking into land, in close proximity.”

He said it was unclear what happened prior to the fall, but there was a possibility they went to hug each other and lost their balance.

Nicky told the inquest her last memory before the fall was being stood face to face, adding: “I remember seeing my feet, flip-flops coming off and just rolling and rolling and rolling.

“I’m guessing he would have given me a hug and that’s what made me stumble back.”



She said when she came round, as she believed she was unconscious, she thought Ben had not fallen and she had just slipped.

“I didn’t know if he panicked, gone to find help, I didn’t even think he’d fell,” she said.

The coroner recorded Ben’s death as an accident, after he fell down the footpath on to the beach below, causing multiple rib fractures.

These injuries caused pulmonary haemorrhage – bleeding in the lungs – which led to respiratory failure.

“Ben was intoxicated with alcohol which contributed to death,” he said.



The inquest, which was attended by his family, heard Ben was described as really funny, someone who adored his children and was a much-loved grandson, son, brother and father.

At the time Ben’s death was announced, tributes from his friends described him as “one of the good ones” and a “great guy”.

Kaci, in her 20s, shared a picture of the pair smiling along with a red love heart.

Clark is also believed to have been a father to a younger daughter.

Becky Paris said: “Honestly I just spent the majority of the evening blabbering on about how ‘it’s the kind of thing you read about in the newspapers, but think well it wouldn’t ever happen’ as it wasn’t real life.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Today I am just absolutely heartbroken for you and your little family.

“No words that could make sense of it. You really were one of the good ones mate.”

News.title: Mum with VERY quirky name makes plea to Sun readers to find mystery 90s TV cop character who inspired it
News.content:
A MUM called Hollie-Popcorn Sanderson is looking for help from Sun readers to find a mystery telly cop character that inspired her quirky name.

The 31-year-old says her mum believes she named her after a female detective called “Lucy Popcorn” from a TV show in the 1990s.



But there is no trace online of the name so she is hoping someone can solve the mystery.

The mum of three has embraced her unusual name — she even has a popcorn-themed wall at her home in Uxbridge, West London.



And she has a tattoo of the cinema snack that says “fresh since 95”.

Hollie-Popcorn insists her name – which many assume is a chosen moniker – serves as an excellent icebreaker and has not held her back professionally.

The British Sign Language teacher uses “Popcorn” as her sign name.

She told The Sun: “When I was a teaching assistant, the teenagers loved it.



“I got tonnes of cards addressed to ‘Miss Popcorn’ when I left.”

She said: “As an adult I absolutely love and embrace my name.”

But she is not a fan of the stuff itself, saying: “I think popcorn’s quite dry.

“It wouldn’t be my choice and I rarely go to the cinema.”

News.title: Shocking moment motorcyclist is flung across car after smashing into bonnet – before sprinting off from crash
News.content:
THIS is the disturbing moment a biker smashed into the bonnet of a car before getting up and – in a twisted turn of events – fleeing the scene in north London.

Police were called to the scene of the crash on Moundfield Road, Stamford Hill, at 5.41pm on Sunday.



Instead of finding the victim, officers recovered “a quantity of drugs” in the aftermath of the collision.

CCTV footage showed how the bizarre incident unfolded on the quiet road.



Moments after the car stopped at a crossing, the bike smashed into its right side.

The man is flung in the air before landing on the asphalt on the other side of the vehicle.

Miraculously, he stands up – seemingly uninjured – and flees the scene on foot, abandoning his bike and one of his shoes.

Behind him, he also leaves a small package that has spilled on the asphalt.



A number of people who witnessed the crash appeared confused about why the man ran away, pointing at his direction.

Officers said they later recovered drugs from the crashed bike that was left behind.

A photo shared on X from the scene of the incident shows an officer holding a clear bag, with evidence inside.

“Enquiries are ongoing and officers are looking for the suspect who fled the scene,” a statement from the police said.

“He is described as white, with short dark hair and was wearing black trousers and a light green top.



“Anyone with information that may assist police is asked to call 101 quoting CAD 5527/16Aug.”

News.title: Net Zero has failed and made YOUR electricity more expensive – here’s my plan to cut bills by £320billion
News.content:
THE definition of insanity is doing the same thing over and over again and expecting a different result.

When it comes to fighting climate change, we have been doing the same thing for years — setting targets, ploughing money into government subsidies and failed schemes, while deindustrialising Britain and sending jobs to China.



We’ve all made massive sacrifices. And, in return, we’ve had steadily hotter summers and rainier winters.

If that isn’t evidence that Net Zero isn’t working, then I don’t know what is.



The targets to cut greenhouse gas emissions, set by Ed Miliband in 2008 and continued by previous Conservative governments, have driven up energy costs, weakened our industrial base and made us more and more dependent on foreign imports with higher emissions.

But they are not solving climate change. In fact, they are making the problem worse by making electricity so expensive barely anyone can afford to adopt clean technologies.



When bills are up, money is tight and people delay green upgrades and are put off buying electric cars or installing heat pumps.

We’ve become a warning to the rest of the world.

A new report, by the think tank Onward in collaboration with the Shadow Energy Secretary Claire Coutinho, says that an electricity grid that prioritised cutting bills instead of Net Zero would save consumers more than £320billion over 20 years, make Britian’s electricity a third cheaper by 2050, and still be nearly 80 per cent clean.

Unlike Labour, who are wedded to the old failing plans, or Reform, who still don’t believe climate change is happening, the Conservatives will bring common sense back to energy policy.



Andy Burnham entered No10 promising to right the wrongs of Keir Starmer.

It was suggested Burnham would approve the new licences for Rosebank and Jackdaw — the oil and gas fields awaiting approval for drilling in the North Sea.

A month later and he seems to be kicking the decision down the road because he’s worried about the “optics”. This is a shameful absence of leadership.

With Burnham pushing ahead with Miliband’s mad plan to ban all new licences, it should come as no surprise that our biggest oil company, BP, has decided to put its North Sea business up for sale.



But they are merely following in the footsteps of refinery operators, chemicals firms, ceramic manufacturers and thousands of other companies who have given up operating in Britain, unable to weather the combination of energy costs and the hostile tax and regulatory environment under Labour.

It just does not have to be like this.

We can care for our environment and move towards clean energy without scorching the earth with taxes, bans and mandates.

Net Zero is a political programme, not a law of nature.



We should preserve our countryside, encourage biodiversity, invest in flood defences and ensure Britain is resilient in the face of a changing climate.

We currently have the highest industrial energy prices in the developed world, and domestic energy prices are increasing at a rate faster than Labour can subsidise them with taxpayer handouts.

Onward’s report exposes just how much extra you are going to have to pay to get Britain to Net Zero.

We will soon be spending billions building pylons and cables, carving up the countryside in the process.

We will have to pay for expensive back up for when the wind’s not blowing. And we’ll pay even more to switch wind farms off when the wind’s blowing too hard.



This is absurdity. All of the costs simply end up on your energy bills.

All this is doing is making electricity expensive so factories shut down here, then move to China which has an exceptionally high rate of approving and building new coal plants or reactivating old ones.

That does not reduce emissions, it just changes where they come from — while costing Britain jobs, investment and prosperity.

The most important thing we can do to protect our industry, to cut bills for families, and to help the environment, is to make electricity as cheap as possible.

All of this is why my Conservative Party has pledged to scrap the carbon tax — the biggest green levy — and scrap the legally binding target for Net Zero by 2050.



That target is suffocating government in legal action by green groups, pushing up bills and strangling business with more and more reporting duties and regulations.

Together, our changes will save families £200 off their electricity bills, give a lifeline to our automotive industry, and revive oil and gas production in the North Sea and all of the jobs it supports in Aberdeen and across the United Kingdom.

This is not just about our economy and jobs, it’s about everyone’s cost of living and quality of life, it’s about common sense.

For instance, the Net Zero rules currently ban installing air conditioning in new homes.

That’s another ban that I’ll scrap, in the interests of all of us who have been suffering sleepless nights and grumpy days in this hot summer.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Onward’s report is just the latest in a bank of research and evidence that we are building to make the case for a complete change of thinking on energy.

No other party is doing this detailed work and no other party is ready to take the tough choices to get Britain working again.

News.title: Scrapping Net Zero power grid drive would leave families £540 a year better off, says Kemi Badenoch
News.content:
FAMILIES could be £540 a year better off if Britain ditches the dash for a fully Net Zero power grid, says Kemi Badenoch.

Scrapping the drive would save £320billion over 20 years, according to the Tories.



A report by the party today reveals using more nuclear and gas, and fewer renewables, would cut electricity system costs by up to almost a third by 2050.

And the electricity generated would still be nearly 80 per cent cleaner.



Tory leader Kemi Badenoch’s Shadow Energy Secretary Claire Coutinho is to present the findings of the report by think-tank Onward and energy advisers Transira Energy.

It says the price of wind and solar fail to reflect extra costs loaded on bills such as pylons, cables and back-up generation when the wind does not blow.



She will blast former Energy Secretary Ed Miliband’s Clean Power 2030 target for trying to remove carbon from electricity generation no matter the cost.

She will also accuse him of axing a full costing of renewable power which she commissioned when Energy Secretary.

She will add: “Conservatives are not in denial about climate change, it’s the Left who are in denial about the fact their climate policy is failing.”

The legally-binding target to hit Net Zero by 2050 was introduced by the Tories in 2019.



Mrs Badenoch says doing so would be impossible without bankrupting Britain.

New Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said the Tories would “tie Britain to the fossil fuel roller-coaster and keep bills higher for families”.

News.title: Three dead after family get into difficulty in sea
News.content:
A spokesperson for Air Ambulance Charity Kent Surrey Sussex said both of its helicopters and critical care team had been sent to the scene as part of the response, and Shoreham RNLI said its lifeboat had been called out.

South East Coast Ambulance Service (Secamb) said it had been called to "reports of four people in need of medical attention".

A section of the A259 â a main commuter road which runs through Brighton, Shoreham and Worthing â was closed.

BBC reporter Callum French said despite warm weather, sea conditions had been "pretty rough" because of high winds, describing the response as "the biggest turnout [of emergency services] I have seen".

Witnesses described seeing large numbers of emergency vehicles and helicopters arriving at the seafront.

Resident Shirley Pumfrey said: "I have never seen them do that. The whole road was just full of emergency services.

"It was horrific and quite scary to see that many."

Steve Chapman, who lives opposite the beach, said he could not get into his road because it was cordoned off.

"There were all sorts of rumours flying around, it was very upsetting," he said.

Another resident, Pete Book, said he had been walking home from the pub when he saw ambulances, coastguard crews and helicopters converging on the area.

Shelley Ayres, who also lives opposite the beach at Shoreham, said: "The sea has been very calm for months and months, but today it has got a lot rougher."

Tom Rutland, East Worthing and Shoreham MP, earlier urged people to stay away from the area while emergency services dealt with the incident.

After news emerged of the deaths, he said his thoughts were with the family and friends of those who had died and he added: "I know the whole community here in Shoreham will be hoping and praying for the recovery of the young girl, external receiving medical treatment in hospital."

Shoreham Port said it was working with multiple agencies and also urged the public to avoid the area.

News.title: 'Everyone in for Christmas' - Burnham unveils rough sleeping plan
News.content:
In an opinion piece in the Guardian, external, Burnham wrote: "For decades, Westminster has treated rough sleeping like a problem to step around rather than solve. It's a philosophy that took hold in the 1980s and came back full force in the era of austerity: this idea that rough sleeping is just a fact of life rather than something government has a responsibility to end...

"No matter who they are or what they've been through, every person sleeping rough deserves a chance to get back on their feet â and, together, that's exactly what we'll give them."

The prime minister said he wanted to build on the success of Everyone In, a Covid pandemic-era scheme that saw thousands of rough sleepers housed in hotels and temporary accommodation.

About 37,000 people were helped by the scheme following its launch in March 2020. The charity Shelter found that about a quarter of them had found settled accommodation, in the form of housing lasting at least six months., external

The announcement comes with an additional Â£102m in new funding, taking Burnham's total commitment to tackling rough sleeping to Â£442m since becoming prime minister. The money is said to be "fully funded" within the Ministry of Housing's budget.

As well as providing immediate support get people off the streets, the funding is also designed to deliver over 1,000 homes over the next three years to provide rough sleepers with permanent accommodation. The funding will also provide "intensive wraparound support," typically psychiatric and drug and alcohol services to help people rebuild their lives.

Burnham says he will organise a special conference in the autumn, inviting business, charities and faith groups to outline how they can help tackle the problem. Councils and mayors will play a leading role in devising local solutions with the areas with the biggest problem receiving the most support.

Jasmine Basran, head of policy at Crisis, said the charity welcomed the announcement and believed an end to rough sleeping was possible.

"What we also want to see in the longer term is interventions to prevent people from being forced to sleep rough in the first place."

She urged departments across government to work together to address the issue - saying too many people being discharged from hospital or leaving care were ending up on the streets.

Sarah Elliott, Shelter's chief executive, called Burnham's pledge a "game-changing move".

She said "tackling the most visible form of homelessness is a strong start" but urged the prime minister to act on his promise to build more council houses to help people living in temporary accommodation.

The shadow housing secretary said Burnham had promised to end rough sleeping while Manchester mayor "and failed because he didn't do the hard work necessary".

James Cleverly added that families would fear there would be tax rises unless Labour could "come clean on what other programmes they are cutting to pay for this project".

Liberal Democrat housing spokesperson Gideon Amos said: "Sticking plasters won't fix the homelessness crisis. Without a proper long-term plan, people could simply find themselves back on the streets once the festive headlines fade."

He urged Burnham to commit to a Lib Dem target to build 150,000 social homes every year.

Deputy Reform UK leader Richard Tice also criticised Burnham's efforts to tackle homelessness while Manchester mayor, and described the government's new plans as "yet another vague announcement with no substances which uses our most vulnerable for political point-scoring".

News.title: Scientists stunned by children's lung recovery in ultra low emission zone
News.content:
Scientists say they have been "stunned" by how quickly young children's lungs began to recover and grow after pollution restrictions were brought in where they lived.

Researchers found that children in London whose lung growth had been stunted by pollution showed impressive improvements after the introduction of an Ultra Low Emission Zone (Ulez) in 2019 reduced emissions.

The study followed more than 3,400 primary school children in London and Luton and provides what scientists believe is the strongest evidence yet that local clean air zones could help reduce some of the harm caused by pollution during childhood.

But independent researchers caution that other factors must also be considered.

Air pollution can stunt the growth of young children's lungs leaving them at an increased risk of asthma, heart disease, diabetes and even premature death.

Children are also more vulnerable to pollution because their lungs and immune systems are still developing. And when outside, they tend to be closer to the ground and nearer sources of exhaust fumes, for example.

In 2020 Ella Adoo-Kissi-Debrah, a nine-year-old girl from London who died following an asthma attack in 2013, became the first person in the UK to have air pollution listed as a cause of death.

In the study, researchers recruited six to nine-year-olds attending primary schools in London's ultra low emission zone and followed the same children for five years, comparing them to similar children (in terms of socio-economic background, physical activity and ethnicity) in Luton.

Children in the study had annual lung function and capacity tests in the year before Ulez came in and for four years after.

Initial results showed children's lungs in London were smaller in capacity than those in Luton, which is less polluted than London but has a similar mix of pollutants.

At the end of the study the children's lung capacity reached near identical levels in both groups.

"While we would expect children's lungs to grow year on year, our results indicate that the London children's lung growth had accelerated during the four years to 'catch up' with the control group in Luton to reach similar levels of lung capacity," researchers say.

"I was absolutely stunned when I first saw the results," Prof Chris Griffiths, a senior author on the study, at Queen Mary University of London, told the BBC.

"The speed of catch up in lung capacity in the London group was surprising and impressive.

"This shows an ambitious clean air zone can drive pollution levels down, rapidly restoring children's stunted lung growth."

The main test measured how much air a child could forcibly breathe out in one second after a big breath in.

In practical terms the improvements could mean children in the London group could run as fast as the Luton group without getting out of breath or blow out of the same number of candles for example, Griffiths explained.

Another way of testing for lung capacity used in the study showed significant improvements too, though not to the same extent - implying there are still gains to be made.

Overall the proportion of children in London whose lung capacity was deemed "clinically impaired" (suggesting lung damage resulting in coughs or breathlessness) fell from 14% to 9%.

In Luton - where some smaller scale measures were put in place to tackle air pollution - the figures were 9% to 7%.

The team's measurements also showed the level of nitrogen dioxide children were exposed to fell faster in London than in Luton over this time.

Researchers say this is key as it likely demonstrates that the improved lung growth they saw was related to air quality improvements following the implementation of Ulez.

London's Ulez was first introduced in 2019 by Mayor Sadiq Khan in a bid to "clean up London's air". London had high levels of the harmful gas nitrogen dioxide which comes from motor vehicles.

Older, more polluting vehicles had to pay a daily charge to drive in central London. The measures were later expanded to cover the whole capital. While many supported the policy it provoked political opposition and protests.

News.title: Camilla admits it was 'difficult' to keep King's cancer diagnosis a secret
News.content:
Queen Camilla has spoken for the first time about King Charles III's cancer diagnosis, describing the pressure of keeping it secret in the early stages of treatment.

In a video to mark the 30th anniversary of Maggie's cancer charity, the Queen, who is president of the charity, recalls how "difficult" it was to avoid discussing her husband's treatment while on an official engagement with cancer patients and their families.

In January 2024, the Queen opened a new Maggie's cancer support centre at the Royal Free Hospital in London.

She had just found out that the King had cancer and would need treatment but had to hold back from telling anyone as the official announcement had not been made public.

"Nobody could say anything at the time, that was quite difficult.

"I almost said something but, you know, I felt that it wasn't the time to say," the Queen told the chief executive of Maggie's, Dame Laura Lee.

"It was just a week before it became public and the courage that must have taken for you," Dame Laura told the Queen - referring to how personally challenging the hospital visit must have been.

"I was just longing to let it out, but obviously I couldn't," the Queen said.

The King's cancer diagnosis was revealed on 5 February 2024, just days after the Queen's engagement at the Royal Free Hospital.

More than two years later, he is still receiving cancer treatment. Buckingham Palace has reiterated that his health continues to move in a "positive direction".

In the seven-minute film recorded at Clarence House, the Queen says the King's way of coping has always been to push on with official duties. She spoke of helping to look after her "poor husband".

"Nothing stopped him. He just said, 'This is my way. I'm going to cope with it,'" she said.

During the hospital visit, the Queen described feeling aware that she was now sharing the experience of so many families she met.

"I was almost questioning them. I didn't want to pry too deeply. But normally when I went in, I was just talking to them, but I don't know, I felt it was much more deep," the Queen said.

"I looked at everybody who was suffering and all the relations and I think it made me realise even more how important these places were."

The King has never disclosed the type of cancer he has, but has engaged widely with those treating and supporting cancer patients.

Maggie's says the King's public announcement prompted a 12% increase in men contacting them with a cancer diagnosis.

"The King's openness about his diagnosis has undoubtedly helped others to be more open themselves, and to now hear the Queen's completely understandable and natural response as a wife shines a light on why it is so important that family and friends also get the support they need," said Dame Laura.

"To hear her speak so powerfully of her own emotions when visiting the Royal Free centre, while knowing about his Majesty's diagnosis, is a huge honour."

Maggie's has 27 centres across the UK, built in the grounds of major NHS cancer hospitals, and supports hundreds of thousands of people each year.

News.title: Is another UK heatwave on the way in September?
News.content:
While wet weather is forecast for many this week, some long-range forecasts are suggesting further dry and sunny spells in September.

Many of us have experienced the first bit of rain in around two months as the weather turned more unsettled on Tuesday.

This change in weather patterns will also bring lower temperatures through this week, perhaps falling to around 2 to 4C below the mid-August average.

The prospect of cooler weather has led to speculation about the possibility of another heatwave - the sixth of the year - developing in September.

News.title: Suspended Reform UK member vows to fight to remain in party
News.content:
Political commentator Tim Montgomerie has told BBC Newsnight he will fight his suspension from Reform UK for criticising senior party figures in media interviews.

He said his appeal against suspension would be a test case of whether Reform could tolerate free speech.

The party said Montgomerie had been suspended in line with its rules after public criticism he made.

Montgomerie is a right-of-centre political commentator who defected from the Conservatives to Reform UK in 2024, and who has seen himself as a critical friend of the party leadership.

But it seems he is now regarded as more of a critic and less of a friend - and has had his party membership suspended.

On Friday, Montgomerie had told the BBC he was frustrated by party leader Nigel Farage's "aggrieved tone" after last week's Clacton by-election.

And on a Spectator podcast on Tuesday, he had said another senior party figure, Zia Yusuf, needed to become a team player and should not act "like a child" in politics.

It is understood his suspension came after the podcast was recorded but before it was released.

"I am going to fight this suspension. I want to stay in Reform. I didn't leave the Conservative Party lightly," he told Newsnight.

"I think Reform can reach parts of the country that the Conservative Party never will be able to so I'm going to fight my corner in Reform and I'm going to make this a test case of whether it is a party that can tolerate free speech and dissent," he added.

Montgomerie said he supported Reform's policies on immigration and welfare, but he has also highlighted internal tensions in the party.

In a video statement on X after news of his suspension emerged on the Guido Fawkes website, Montgomerie said he was only trying to make the party "better and stronger" with his public criticisms.

He added that Farage did not know about the decision to suspend him, and he had warned the Reform leader when he joined the party that he would be critical at times, as he had been of the Tory leadership when he ran the ConservativeHome website.

Reform's leadership will have to decide whether it is more politically difficult to rescind rather than to retain Montgomerie's party membership.

News.title: Deaf patient given wrong jab due to sign language error, report says
News.content:
A deaf woman was given the wrong vaccine because she was not provided with a British Sign Language (BSL) interpreter at her doctor's surgery, a report says.

The Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman (PHSO) said disabled people were being let down by inaccessible communications.

It said the patient, Samantha, had booked a flu jab but was instead given a Covid vaccine after staff failed to show her a BSL video which would have highlighted the error. She said the experience had had a "profound impact" on her.

The Department of Health and Social Care said the "deeply upsetting stories" were "completely unacceptable" and NHS and social care organisations had a duty to make services accessible.

The PHSO investigates complaints about UK government departments, public organisations and the NHS in England.

It said public services were legally required to support people with their accessible communication needs, which might be due to a disability, neurodivergence or English not being their first language.

Samantha had booked her flu and Covid jabs for separate weeks and showed a nurse a note on her phone which said she was there for the "flu jab only", the PHSO said.

Despite that, the practice said it believed it had correctly established Samantha wanted the Covid vaccine and had got her consent through her grandmother, even though she had early-stage dementia and was not in the treatment room.

Following an investigation, the PHSO recommended the surgery should apologise and pay Samantha Â£450. It has also since signed a contract with a sign language interpreting company.

The NHS Northamptonshire Integrated Care Board said it was "very sorry" about Samantha's experience, and that it expected practices to make "reasonable adjustments to support effective communication".

The PHSO said it had found disabled people risked not getting vital information about their healthcare, finances or employment because of a lack of accessible formats such as large print or audio materials.

Since April 2020, it said it had concluded 623 investigations related to reasonable adjustments, of which 496 were upheld or partly upheld.

The report also highlighted the case of Alan Graham, who was deaf and was being treated for cancer at University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Trust.

When an interpreter was not available, hospital staff asked his teenage grandson to interpret for the family and tell Graham's deaf daughter that he might die.

News.title: Mobile payments on the rise but cash decline slows
News.content:
Consumers are increasingly relying on their mobile phone to make payments rather than carrying bank cards, new data shows.

Two-thirds of adults in the UK were registered with at least one mobile payment service last year, according to an annual report by banking trade body UK Finance.

Use of a phone to pay has jumped in recent years. It is a decade since Apple Pay was launched in the UK.

While cash use continues to decline, the data suggests that the fall is slowing and that notes and coins will remain an important payment option for many people a decade from now.

Consumers are increasingly storing card details on phones or watches and making contactless payments backed up by facial or fingerprint verification, instead of pressing in a PIN.

Nine in 10 users of mobile wallets have their debit card loaded as their default payment method on their phone, with the remainder having registered their credit card.

News.title: Join EU migration pact to tackle small boats, says Ed Davey
News.content:
The UK should join the EU's new Migration and Asylum Pact as a way of tackling small boat crossings across the Channel, Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey has said.

The agreement, which came into force in June, aims to speed up the asylum process, increase the number of irregular migrants returned to their home countries and spread responsibility for asylum seekers across the EU.

Sir Ed argues that signing up to the pact would allow the UK to return asylum seekers to the first EU country they entered, thereby "destroying the business model" of the gangs behind the crossings.

Labour said the government's efforts to work with European countries to tackle small boat crossings were "bearing fruit".

A Labour spokesperson said more than 47,000 crossings had been prevented in two years and 70,000 people with no right to be in the UK had been removed.

"There's more to do and that will only happen by working in collaboration with the EU," the spokesperson added.

So far this year, more than 14,000 people have arrived in the UK by small boat - a fall of 43% compared to the previous year.

The EU's new pact, which was nearly 10 years in the making, introduces mandatory screening and an updated database to track those arriving in the bloc.

Under the rules, EU nations must take in migrants from those member states that see the highest number of arrivals - such as Italy and Greece - or instead provide extra funding or resources.

News.title: Burnham received £345,000 of donations ahead of becoming PM
News.content:
Andy Burnham has registered accepting Â£345,000 of donations over the past year including Â£164,347 from businessman Lord Sainsbury.

The donations, listed in the most recent version of the MPs' register of interests,, external are the prime minister's first declarations since he was elected to Parliament in June.

Separately, Burnham has also listed hospitality and gifts he received in the year before he returned to Parliament, including trips to Glastonbury, Lancashire Cricket Club and the Aintree Racecourse.

A Labour Party spokesperson said: "It's right that political campaigns are funded by the generous support of party donors, rather than via the public purse.

"All declarations have been made in line with Parliamentary and Electoral Commission rules."

New MPs are required to register all their current financial interests, and any registrable benefits (other than earnings) received in the 12 months before their election within one month of their election.

Lord Sainsbury's donations went towards Burnham's campaign to become Labour leader. Businessman Gary Lubner and former Greater Manchester night-time economy tsar Sacha Lord donated Â£25,000 and Â£35,000 to the campaign respectively.

The TV production company Charlie Parsons Creative contributed Â£50,000 and the think tank ThinkLabour, formerly known as Labour Together, provided Â£22,186.

The donations included the provision of office space, IT equipment, staffing, polling, travel, social media support and message testing.

Burnham's list also includes Â£20,000 of donations towards mayoral campaigning from the trade unions Unison, the Communications Workers Union and the Fire Brigades Union.

Labour peer Lord Blunkett appears on the list having donated Â£2,000 towards Burnham's campaign to become the MP for Makerfield.

Gifts and hospitality Burnham accepted when he was mayor of Greater Manchester include:

Four tickets to Glastonbury, where he was speaking at an event, from the festival organisers and Â£1,000 for accommodation from the campaigning group PRS for Music

Tickets worth Â£3,800 to the Brit Awards in Manchester from Sony Music Entertainment

Two tickets worth Â£500 for the Aintree Racecourse from the Jockey Club Racecourse

Two tickets, valued at Â£458, from Lancashire Cricket Club for a game in The Hundred tournament

A hamper basket and Wedgewood tea set worth Â£340 from the ambassador of Qatar

Shortly after becoming prime minister in 2024, Sir Keir Starmer became embroiled in a row over the gifts he had accepted including tickets to a Taylor Swift concert and thousands of pounds for clothes.

He subsequently paid back more than Â£6,000 worth of gifts and hospitality. He also tightened the rules so that serving ministers had to consider "the need to maintain the public's confidence in the standard of propriety" when accepting gifts.

News.title: Fire engulfs London waste centre
News.content:
About 100 firefighters are tackling a massive blaze at a waste facility in south-east London.

Fifteen fire engines were called to Landmann Way in Bermondsey shortly before 20:00 BST after about 50 tonnes of household waste caught fire.

London Fire Brigade (LFB) warned that a large amount of smoke was being produced by the blaze and advised local residents to keep their doors and windows closed.

LFB said the cause of the fire was not yet known, but firefighters tackled a blaze at the same facility in June.

Speaking from the scene, station commander Duncan Rees said: "Crews are working hard in difficult conditions to bring the fire under control."

He added that a 32m ladder and a 64m ladder were being used to tackle the flames from above.

Crews from East Greenwich, Old Kent Road, Deptford and surrounding fire stations were dispatched to the scene.

The LFB said it was likely to be a "protracted incident" and crews would work overnight to bring the fire under control.

Rail services into London Bridge from New Cross have been affected due to the fire blocking railway lines, National Rail said.

"Trains between these stations may be cancelled, severely delayed by up to 100 minutes or revised," it added.

Rachael Jardine, a freelance journalist based in New Cross, told BBC London that trains on a nearby Overground track were continuing to pass despite the "thick black smoke".

A local resident said he had first spotted the blaze while cycling home.

"I was coming back from Tescos and I could see the smoke from the road," he said.

"We cycled back to mine and realised it was just across the road... it's pretty mental."

News.title: British couple on honeymoon killed in helicopter crash on Greek island
News.content:
A young British couple and their pilot were killed in a helicopter crash on the Greek island of Sifnos on Monday, Greek police have said.

They have been named as newlyweds Alexander Cromie and Marie Ebert, who were in Greece on their honeymoon.

The private Bell 206 helicopter crashed just metres from a landing pad, killing the pair and their pilot, a Greek national.

The couple are said to have taken the helicopter from the village of Markopoulo near Athens to the popular holiday island, Kathimerini reported.

Greece's aviation safety authority told the BBC it was investigating the crash and that its investigators were heading to the scene on Tuesday to gather evidence and speak to witnesses.

News.title: Prevent not helping children fixated with violence, children's commissioner says
News.content:
The government's counter-extremism programme is not able to deal with the growing number of children being referred to it who are "fixated on violence without a clear ideology", the children's commissioner has said.

Referrals of children to Prevent have risen over the past decade - from 2,918 in 2016-17 to 4,715 in 2024-25 - and Dame Rachel de Souza said most were being sent back to schools without further action.

Dame Rachel said most children being referred did not identify with traditional forms of extremism and "stronger safeguarding" was needed for this group.

The government said it was reviewing the report and developing further options to "manage those fascinated with extreme violence".

Dame Rachel's report comes just over two years after three girls were killed while attending a dance class in Southport in July 2024.

Their attacker Axel Rudakubana was 17 at the time and had himself been referred to Prevent three times between 2019 and 2021 due to his interest in terrorist attacks and school shootings, but his case too had been closed because he did not have a clear ideology.

Prevent was set up 20 years ago to try to identify future potential terrorists and intervene in their lives, often by challenging hateful ideologies such as far right extremism or support for jihadist violence.

The second phase of the Southport Inquiry is examining how to deal with individuals who pose a risk of extreme violence but where ideology is not the primary driver, as well as the role of the internet and social media in influencing and enabling them.

A Prevent referral is one made to the police when there are concerns that a person may be susceptible to radicalisation or could be at risk of becoming involved in or supporting terrorism. Typically, for children, this process starts with potential concerning behaviour spotted by teachers or social workers.

Most child referrals are made by the education sector including schools - 60% in the year from April 2024 to March 2025.

The report by the children's commissioner found that most of these referrals were being sent back to the education sector because Prevent was not able to effectively deal with their cases - because its focus was on the risk of terrorism which generally means violence being carried out for an ideological objective.

Some 71% of child referrals were found to have "no specific extremist ideology identified".

Dame Rachel told the BBC many cases were linked to children being involved in the "most awful online communities, watching other children self-harm and trying to make them do that, obsessed with killers and school shootings" - material she said was illegal under the Online Safety Act.

"Counter-terrorism police and Prevent are excellent at deprogramming children who have been caught into ideological movements," she told BBC Radio 4's World at One programme.

"What they can't deal with is this, so we have to make sure there is a far wider response."

News.title: Two more officers arrested in Police Federation fraud investigation
News.content:
Four more people, including two serving police officers, have been arrested as part of an investigation into suspected fraud and bribery at the Police Federation of England and Wales.

Two men and two women were arrested at the federation's offices in Leatherhead, Surrey, on Tuesday. The women are both in their 50s and the men in their 40s and 50s.

The City of London Police's corruption unit, which leads on fraud investigations, said all four suspects had been taken to a police station for questioning. It comes after three arrests connected to the same case were made in March.

The Police Federation represents more than 145,000 rank-and-file officers, up to and including the rank of chief inspector as well as special constables.

Det Supt Jim Halkett said the investigation "continues to make significant progress, with officers working through a number of lines of inquiry to establish the full facts and circumstances surrounding this case".

Police said the four people arrested on Tuesday were being questioned on suspicion of fraud by abuse of position of trust. One of the women and the man in his 50s were also being held on suspicion of bribery and fraud by failing to disclose.

It comes after the three men were arrested in March on suspicion of fraud by abuse of position - a 51-year-old from Wales, a 55-year-old from Bristol and a 46-year-old from Surrey.

Police said the three either currently or previously "occupied senior roles within [the Police Federation's] governance and operational structure".

Police Federation chief executive Mukund Krishna is understood to be among the three. The federation confirmed he was suspended from his role "due to an ongoing police investigation" in a statement issued days after the arrests.

News.title: Burnham says he's not embarrassed about hoax message exchange
News.content:
Andy Burnham says he is not embarrassed that he exchanged messages with a person posing as US President Donald Trump's chief of staff.

The prime minister added all politicians face "these challenges" but insisted he did "everything right" in how he handled the security breach.

News website Politico first reported, external that Burnham communicated with a person claiming to be Susie Wiles. Burnham said there was a "minimal exchange of information of zero consequence".

Liberal Democrat MP James MacCleary has written to Parliament's Intelligence and Security Committee (ISC) to ask them to consider investigating what he called an "egregious security breach".

It is understood the communication between Burnham and the person posing as Wiles was in the form of messages and there was no conversation between the two.

Asked if he was embarrassed about the incident, Burnham told broadcasters: "No, I am not because there was a minimal exchange, nothing of consequence and quickly I realised that this needed to be reported and I did so.

"So I handled it in the right way. All politicians are receiving these pressures and these challenges, but I did everything right."

Pressed on what action is being taken to find out who was behind the incident and to improve systems, Burnham said the "correct action" had been taken both in the UK and the US, without providing further details.

MacCleary, in his letter to ISC chairman Lord Beamish, said the security of the prime minister's communications "ought to be an absolute priority".

He added: "We need to understand how this breach could occur, or else risk it being repeated."

News.title: Nigeria influencer arrested after seizure of cocaine worth $28m destined for the UK
News.content:
The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) said 184.5kg of cocaine was found concealed in brown boxes at a courier facility in Lagos on Monday 3 August.

The agency said it was being exported by an international trafficking network that for years had used Nigeria as a transit hub to move drugs to the UK, other parts of Europe and to Asia.

Micheal was arrested 10 days later at Lagos's Murtala Mohammed International Airport as he attempted to leave the country on a business-class flight to the French capital.

"Upon credible intelligence that he intended to flee the countryâ¦ our operatives moved decisively and apprehended him at the boarding gateâ¦ just as he attempted to escape the reach of the law," the head of the NDLEA, General Buba Marwa, said.

Micheal was carrying more than $12,840 in cash in three currencies - euros, pounds and naira - as well as expensive jewellery "consistent with the proceeds of his illicit trade" when he was arrested, the agency said.

A second detained suspect, Lawal Mujab Kehinde, is alleged to have been a staff member of a logistics company through which the cocaine was transported.

The NDLEA alleged the 33-year-old packaged cocaine for export and was paid in cash. Kehinde has not commented on the allegations or been charged in court.

The agency said other suspected members of the network in the UK have also been arrested by counterpart law enforcement agencies overseas.

The BBC is chasing the UK authorities for comment.

Marwa said the arrests demonstrated what could be achieved when international agencies worked together and vowed to pursue other members of the network.

"We will track you to the departure gates if we must," he said at a news conference in Lagos.

News.title: I love solo holidays, so why do so many people think it’s weird to go on one?
News.content:

When you tell someone you’re going on holiday, nobody ever asks why. Unless you happen to be going on holiday alone, and then it’s almost always the first thing they’ll say. The words are usually accompanied by pitying eyes and a concerned tone of voice, because if you’re going away alone, the assumption is that something has gone terribly wrong. Like you’ve been dumped, lost your job, or entered into an existential crisis that can only be cured by a year of nomadic solo living (thank you, Eat, Pray, Love).

These reasons aside, why else would you dare to travel solo? Well, as someone who has been away on her own several times in the last few years, allow me to educate you. Because once you start travelling this way, trust me, you will want to do it again – and may begin to wonder why you ever travelled with anyone at all.

The first time was out of necessity: a long weekend in Paris I’d originally booked for me and my boyfriend. We broke up. I couldn’t get any money back on the trip. So I went alone. The first dinner was, admittedly, a little bit teary. But the following day, I was writing in a cafe when someone I went to school with randomly walked past.

We ended up having the most fun night out together that ended in a karaoke bar with a group of French students. That wouldn’t have happened had I not been on my own.

Since then, I’ve gone away a few times of my own volition: a week in Santorini, a few days in Provence, and a stint in Lisbon. Every time, I’ve come away feeling peaceful and restored. Much more so than when I’ve gone away with other people. Once you overcome the initial society-induced stigma, there’s something deeply satisfying about being on holiday alone.

open image in gallery Olivia Petter on a solo trip to Santorini in 2022 ( Olivia Petter/The Independent )

There are no schedules to abide by, no dietary requirements dictating your choice of restaurant, and no idle chatter to engage in on the beach when you’d much rather be sunbathing and reading in silence.

As an anxious freelancer whose iPhone is practically glued to her right hand in case of a last-minute work opportunity, I’m someone who struggles to switch off. Going away alone is one of the only things that allows me to do just that. I can exercise, read, and sit in silence with my own thoughts, allowing my nervous system to fully decompress.

Currently, I’m single, which makes travelling alone more of a necessity, perhaps, than it would be if I were in a relationship. But I know I’d still want to go away on my own even if I had a partner – we all need time to ourselves. As an only child, I’m particularly reliant on it in a relationship. It’s the antithesis to what Jamie Oliver and his wife Jools would suggest – the couple has filmed an advertising campaign for the app Life360, which is designed for family members and couples to track one another’s locations. I can’t think of anything worse.

While there may be safety reasons behind using a tracking service, I feel like there is something odd about being so bound to your partner that you feel compelled to track their location 24/7. This is the kind of behaviour apps like this facilitate, whether intentionally or not. For me, it will always be important to have travel autonomy, regardless of whether or not I’m in a relationship.

While friends in relationships say they'd never “let” their partner go away on their own without them; it would feel like a rejection. I think going away alone is a healthy and necessary part of life. It’s a privilege if you can do it and can be empowering, too, as a single woman

If the thought of solo dining sends shivers down your spine, book a cabin or cottage so you get privacy, space to work on that book or creative project Molly Cooper, co-founder of Curated Spaces

If I have one summer without a holiday alone, I start to get twitchy. This is the point I’m at as I write this. Except I cannot decide for the life of me where to go. That’s one catch about travelling alone: you have nobody to bounce ideas off of; the choices are entirely yours and yours alone. This is great, but also totally paralysing, particularly in my current, rather burnt-out, state, where making any kind of decision feels impossibly difficult. Do I go to Granada for a few days to double up on a research trip for a project? Do I find a seaside hotel somewhere in Italy? What about Greece? Isn’t Greece always great?

There are some limitations and personal preferences that make the choice easier: firstly, I cannot drive. So, like many solo travellers, I need somewhere that has everything I need within walking distance. Secondly, I’m more of a beach than a pool person. I don’t have children and would rather not hear or see other people’s while on holiday – sorry. That means an adult-only hotel is ideal. But I also don’t want to be surrounded by couples, which rules out a few overly romantic spots.

These are my parameters – where you want to go on your solo trip will depend on yours. “Be honest about what you’re looking for,” suggests Molly Cooper, co-founder of Curated Spaces, a travel booking platform and community based on personal recommendations. “If the thought of solo dining sends shivers down your spine, book a cabin or cottage so you get privacy, space to work on that book or creative project, and no awkward table-for-one moments.”

Alternatively, if you’re looking to make new friends, Cooper suggests booking a pub with rooms or a small guesthouse. “Somewhere small and family-run is ideal, because the owners will point you to the local spots you'd never find otherwise,” she adds. If you’re thinking of a hotel, try seeking one out that has a communal lounge, café, rooftop, coworking area or organised activities.

open image in gallery Solo trips can take many forms – but the great part is you only need to cater to your own tastes ( Getty/iStock )

“This can give you the chance to meet people without being forced to socialise,” says LP Maurice, travel expert and backpacker. “The Social Hub in San Sebastián is a good example, as it blends private hotel rooms with co-working and communal spaces. If you are comfortable staying in hostels, they can also be a good option for solo travellers. Koba Hostel in San Sebastián is close to the beach and offers shared and private accommodation, while Impact Beach House in Estoril in Lisbon is near several beaches and provides women-only dorms and common areas.”

Those looking to travel alone but in groups should seek out companies like WeRoad and FlashPack, which offer tours tailored to solo travellers. I’ve done one to Mexico with WeRoad before, and it was brilliant. Then there’s Club Avandra, which is a private members travel club designed specifically for women who want to travel in small groups.

Prioritising ourselves and our own wellbeing in a work-obsessed, screen-addicted world is not something to be sneered at

For this particular trip, I want to be left alone. I always head to Mr and Mrs Smith, a booking platform featuring a carefully curated group of uniquely stunning properties, with good perks for regular users, too. My focus this time around is on unpretentious hotels near the beach in quiet places. Sicily looks appealing, as does Paros. I’m yet to book anything but have my eyes on a few that might fit the bill: watch this space.

I’m still not entirely sure where I’ll end up, but I’m making it a priority. And when someone tells me they’re going away alone, I make sure I never ask them why. Instead, I reply, “Well done.” Because prioritising ourselves and our own wellbeing in a work-obsessed, screen-addicted world is not something to be sneered at. It should be celebrated.

News.title: ‘Prolier-than-thou!’ Burnham accused of ‘desperate’ attempt to play up working class roots by novelist
News.content:

Andy Burnham has been accused of being “prolier-than-thou” by using his working class roots to win votes.

Political novelist Robert Harris, a lifelong Labour supporter, has told The Independent he deplores attempts by the prime minister to appear more ‘proletarian’ than he is.

Harris called it a “prolier-than-thou” attitude - political slang based on the phrase ‘holier-than-thou’ - a hypocrite who claims they are more authentically working class than others.

Since entering No 10, Burnham has talked often of his background as a working class Catholic Northerner and feeling “an imposter” at Cambridge University as a result.

Harris, brought up in a council house and who also studied at Cambridge, said he “hated” it when politicians like Burnham “turn on the system that created them” and claimed to have had an “awful” background.

Labour statesmen of the past like 1960s Home Secretary Roy Jenkins had far more genuinely poor origins but never used it to boost their popularity, said Harris.

He also argued Burnham’s “desire to be liked” risked making him look “facile and glib” and forecast public “disillusion” in him could set in soon.

In an in-depth interview with The Independent editor-in-chief Geordie Greig for Independent TV, Harris spoke for the first time of his “painful” rift with Britain’s former ambassador to the US Peter Mandelson after he was forced to resign over the Jeffrey Epstein scandal.

Watch Geordie Greig’s full interview with author Robert Harris below

He reveals that he and Lord Mandelson, godfather to one of Harris’ children, had had no contact of any kind since shocking details of Mandelson’s links to paedophile Epstein emerged earlier this year.

The fact that neither had reached out to the other “speaks volumes”, says Harris.

He discloses a hilarious ‘Fawlty Towers’ style ‘don’t mention the war’ incident at dinner with Tony Blair and wife Cherie at No 10 when Harris fell out with Blair over the 2003 Iraq War.

Harris tips home secretary Shabana Mahmood to become Labour’s first female prime minister - and suggests Burnham’s surprise choice of “malleable” John Healey as chancellor may have been because “formidable” Mahmood intimidates him.

Harris, author of Fatherland, and Conclave, was speaking in the run up to the publication later this month of his latest novel, Agrippa, about the right hand man to Roman Emperor Augustus.

Explaining why he objects to the way he says Burnham and Starmer have played up their working class beginnings Harris says: “Andy Burnham (has) talked about… (he was) very prolier-than-thou about his Labour roots - like Keir Starmer going on about his toolmaker father and all of this rather desperate stuff.”

British statesman Roy Jenkins, former Labour minister who served as president of the European Commission, was born to a miner father who was jailed for his political views - but Jenkins never tried to capitalise on it, states Harris.

open image in gallery Political novelist Robert Harris in conversation with Geordie Greig ( The Independent )

He adds: “I went to Cambridge from a comprehensive school. The system worked for me as it did for Burnham. I hate Labour politicians turning on the very system that's created them.

Harris fears Burnham’s administration will “soon run into problems”.

“He is a deft politician. I think he'll ride the waves very skilfully. Whether he will be able to tackle the fundamental problems in the country, I don't know.

“As so often, his weaknesses and strengths are often just the same trait. He has a desire to be liked, knows how to make people like him and knows how to communicate with people.

“At the same time this can make him look rather glib, facile, and willing to bend… he'll say something to get out of trouble in a tight spot, and then won't be able to follow through. So there will be a process of disillusion - it seems hard to think that there wouldn't be.”

Burnham’s rates cut for pubs was an attempt to woo Labour voters who had defected to Reform, led by beer drinking Nigel Farage, argues Harris, but it was “old fashioned” to see pubs as working class.

“One of the great things about Blair was I thought he had taken class out of politics. I mean, he was a public schoolboy leading (the Labour Party).”

Harris hesitates, clearly troubled, when asked if he has been in touch with Mandelson.

“It's a very painful subject, personal subject,” he says.

“I haven't spoken to him. He hasn't called me or got in touch since he was sacked as ambassador. So that's where we stand. I haven't got in touch with him. He hasn't got in touch with me. I can't say any more than that. I think that merely that speaks volumes.”

Pressed further he says: “I don't want to add to his troubles. People watching or reading this can guess the state of play.”

open image in gallery Robert Harris was reluctant to discuss his friendship with Peter Mandelson ( The Independent )

It sounds as though the friendship is broken for ever.

Reflecting on the wider aspect of the Mandelson-Epstein scandal, Harris says he hates seeing politicians “hunted down by the mob” - just as they were in the time of Agrippa in Rome.

But it also illustrates what motivated him as an author: “It shows you why it's so interesting to write about power… this combination of morality, law, power, personal weakness, personal strength, the drama of it.”

Harris says Starmer’s downfall was caused by his weakness and because he lacked “the ferocity of convictions” that a leader like Margaret Thatcher had, or the ability ‘to see something through once he'd settled on it.

“He buckled again and again. The problem for Starmer was purely personality, I don't think he could get on terms with a lot of his Cabinet.”

Harris sees parallels between the Roman Empire, the frequent subject of his novels, and modern politics.

So called “strong man” leaders such as Trump and Putin were like Emperor Augustus, “essentially dictators” who used power to make themselves rich.

In a more benign fashion, Harris says there was “definitely something of the Agrippa-Augustus relationship” to the alliance between Blair and his Chancellor, and later successor as PM, Gordon Brown.

Brown was “blunt, direct, brooding” - like Agrippa: Blair was “the charming, younger, slighter, front man” - like Augustus.

Harris concedes he had such a “close liaison” with Blair when Labour came to power in 1997 he was effectively part of ‘Team Blair’ - for a while.

He and wife Gill Hornby, also a novelist, were early guests at Chequers, the prime minister’s official country residence in Buckinghamshire, and he and Blair “got on well”.

But he and Blair became “too close” says Harris, recalling how their friendship ended in acrimony over the Iraq War, which Harris strongly opposed.

After early foreign policy successes, Blair foolishly “thought he could walk on water”, says Harris. After Harris made his views clear, Blair tried to patch things up, inviting Harris and his wife to another private dinner with him and Cherie, this time at No 10. Blair appealed to him: “Come on, we, we should get together.”

But the dinner backfired. Harris says: “It was clear that this gamble (the Iraq War) was failing badly.”

open image in gallery Harris said he became ‘too close’ to Tony and Cherie Blair ( Andrew Parsons/PA Wire )

To his surprise the war was raised not by Blair but by Cherie, who announced France’s President Jacques Chirac “had behaved appallingly because he'd opposed the war”.

Blair tried to stop her. “Tony said, ‘Now, don't let's get onto the war’. You know, it was like- Don't…”

I completed the sentence for Harris: “… don’t mention the war?” - as in the famous Fawlty Towers TV series where hotel owner Basil Fawlty (John Cleese) tries - and fails - not to mention the war to a German guest.

Harris laughs: “Yes, it was a touch of Fawlty Towers.”

It led Harris to re-assess Cherie Blair’s political leanings: “She’d always been painted as the leftier of the two, (but she) actually had called round Labour MPs to urge them to support the war.

The ‘froideur’ with Blair continued, but the episode had the benefit of inspiring one of Harris’ most successful novels, The Ghost - more than loosely based on Blair and the Iraq War - and a movie version starring Pierce Brosnan and Ewan McGregor.

It is about a British ex prime minister mired in scandal over a controversial foreign policy collaboration with America. Blair himself was far from pleased.

“He said to my publisher, ‘the next time Robert writes a book tell him to make it up, find his own character’.”’

By contrast Cherie was amused.

“It was quite funny because… her role, the ex-Prime Minister's wife, was played by Olivia Williams. She saw Olivia at some reception and said, ‘Oh, I've seen you playing me in the film’.

“Olivia said, ‘I hope it wasn't too upsetting.’ She said, ‘No, I got to sleep with Pierce Brosnan and Ewan McGregor!’”

While he is lukewarm about Burnham, Harris glows with admiration for home secretary Shabana Mahmood, whom he has met.

“She is blunt, plain speaking, clever, charismatic, talked like a human being, very much what Tony was like at the beginning.

“And she's got a lot of courage, as Tony had. I wouldn't be surprised if she doesn't end up as Labour's first female leader.”

Mahmood is “head and shoulders above” most of the rest of the Cabinet.

Harris, who remains well connected in Labour circles, observes mischievously: “I heard that Burnham backed off making her Chancellor because she's too formidable, she wouldn't be pushed around. He’s got a more malleable figure (as Chancellor) in John Healey.”

An intriguing theory.

Harris is proud of the fact that he has never once voted Conservative and claims the Party could be out of power for decades because of Boris Johnson.

“He could have ruined it (the Tory Party) for a generation. Once you start throwing away the rules and adopt a Trumpian approach to morality and lying then something goes out of politics.”

One of themes in Agrippa is how the huge power of Roman leaders could turn them into monsters.

open image in gallery Harris' latest novel, Agrippa ( PA )

“If you want to look at power, really you can do little better than to go to the Roman world because it's all stripped down and simple.”

The personal consequences of winning and losing power in modern British politics are less violent, but not so different in essence according to Harris.

“You have to take decisions quite ruthlessly. You have to often drop old colleagues, old friends. Look at the bloodletting that's in the Cabinet just lately with Burnham coming in.

“A lot of people will feel that Burnham is a monster, just as a lot of people thought that Starmer was when he fired so many.

“It is a very difficult thing to become a successful politician and not turn into a monster. Harold Wilson (Labour Prime Minister in the 1960s and 1970s) said the trick was to learn to take criticism, harden yourself, absorb it or ignore it, but not to become a monster.

“That is a fine line.”

Strictly Come Dancing’s Amy Dowden has opened up about her health ahead of her return after receiving cancer treatment on screen during Celebrity Hunted.

The professional dancer, 36, was diagnosed with breast cancer three years ago and has since undergone two mastectomies and chemotherapy. She also contracted sepsis and broke her foot.

As documented in the recent series of Celebrity Hunted, Dowden returns to hospital once a month for preventative treatment. She competed on the reality show, which is currently airing on Channel 4, alongside Strictly co-star Carlos Gu.

Despite how emotional the scene was to viewers at home, Dowden has since told The Independent that she now feels comfortable speaking about her treatment on screen.

“I don’t really find it hard now revisiting it because I’m at the hospital once a month,” she said.

open image in gallery Amy Dowden and Carlos Gu on 'Celebrity Hunted' ( Channel 4 )

“It's part of my routine now. I celebrate now how far I've come, how strong I feel, how healthy I am, and I'm just grateful really, and honoured to feel this way,” she continued.

“I’m forever in gratitude to the wonderful healthcare workers who've looked after me, the nurses, doctors, you name it, every healthcare worker. They are our true unsung heroes.”

Both Dowden and Gu are confirmed to be returning to Strictly Come Dancing for its 2026 series, with the full celebrity line-up now officially revealed. While the Welsh pro returned to Strictly in 2024, she was forced to pull out of the series after collapsing due to a foot injury and the following year, she was first out of the competition after celebrity partner Thomas Skinner received the fewest votes from the public.

As for how she’s feeling before the series launch, Dowden said: “Honestly, I feel the fittest, the healthiest, the strongest I’ve ever been, Carlos knows you've just been on tour with me. How would you say I am?”

Carlos responded: “I feel like everything that she went through somehow made her stronger mentally and physically. It made her realise she loves dancing, coming back and dancing and being on stage. We finished touring a month ago and she was was just incredible.

“She looked the best and she feels the best. I think being through something so severe makes you cherish what you have more.”

Dowden went on to explain that the absence of Strictly and dancing in her life has made her “appreciate everything even more”.

“What Carlos and I certainly cemented throughout our time on the run is our friendship and I think now, we're family now for life,” she said. “I think if you can get through Celebrity Hunted together, you can get through anything.”

open image in gallery The 'Strictly' stars are taking part in 'Celebrity Hunted' ( Channel 4 )

In March, Dowden revealed that she almost abandoned her dance career after undergoing treatment for breast cancer, but Gu stopped her from giving it up. “My body had been through everything so I knew I wasn’t who I was, and I was ready to hang up my dancing shoes and my husband and my dear friend, Carlos Gu... said ‘no’," she told Matt Willis’s podcast On The Mend in March. “’Cancer’s taken so much, it’s not taking your dancing back. You can do this.’”

The pair are still in the running to win Celebrity Hunted, competing against the likes of EastEnders’ Brian Conley and his daughter Lucy, Olympian JJ Chalmers and TV presenter Sophie Morgan, and brother-and-sister duo Scarlette and Stuart Douglas.

So far, the hunters have managed to catch Love Island stars Chris Taylor and Toby Aromolaran, and comedians Jen Brister and Laura Smyth.

“You’ve got to be on your game all the time,” Dowden said of the show’s atmosphere. “It’s emotional, intense, stressful as well as learning so much about one another and the generosity of the public.”

Gu added: “This experience really humbles you as a human. You learn so much from each other and you learn so much about yourself. You don’t need much to live because I loved the finer things in life – bags, clothes, good holidays – but you learn that it takes nothing to be kind and to give love.”

Celebrity Hunted continues on Mondays and Tuesdays at 9pm on Channel 4.

Brace yourself Slow Horses fans: Sid Baker is back.

After four years of wondering whether the sharp-witted MI5 agent had truly seen the last of Slough House, viewers finally have their answer.

Olivia Cooke is set to reprise her role as Sidonie “Sid” Baker in the forthcoming sixth season of the Apple TV spy drama, bringing back one of the show’s most conspicuous loose ends.

Cooke’s character was last seen in season one during which she was apparently killed by a bullet to the head. Despite that, speculation as to whether she could return has continued to grow ever since spurred on by Christopher Chung’s Roddy Ho telling Jack Lowden’s River that he had uncovered evidence to suggest Sid may still be alive.

open image in gallery Olivia Cooke in ‘Slow Horses’ as Sid Baker ( Apple TV )

Now those hopes have been answered in the first trailer of the show’s sixth series. Released on Tuesday (18 August), the two-minute clip begins with Gary Oldman’s Jackson Lamb questioning Kristen Scott Thomas’s Diana Taverner over the deaths of his team.

Sid crops up in the final moments of the trailer as she greets Lowden’s character, saying: “Hello, River.”

Of course, this revelation won’t come as a shock to readers of Mick Herron’s books, on which the series is based, but for everyone else Cooke’s return will be a welcome surprise.

In addition to giving fans a glimpse of Sid, the trailer also briefly shows Paul Higgins, who looks to be back in his season one role, Struan Loy.

The synopsis for the forthcoming series reads: “Season 6 sees the Slow Horses on the run as Diana Taverner embroils them all in a fatally high-stakes game of retaliation and revenge.”

open image in gallery Jack Lowden in ‘Slow Horses’ ( Apple TV+ )

Cooke’s return comes in a moment of change for the hit series, with this coming season being the first without long-time showrunner Will Smith, whose exit was announced last year. Gaby Chiappe will be stepping in.

The returning cast includes Oldman, Lowden, Chung, Thomas, Saskia Reeves, Rosalind Eleazar, Joanna Scanlan, and Aimee-Ffion Edwards.

Lowden is among the rumoured frontrunners to be the next James Bond, with many speculating that his stint as a spy on Slow Horses impressed the new 007 casting director Nina Gold, who incidentally also cast the Apple TV drama.

Also joining the cast this time around is Am I Being Unreasonable? star Lenny Rush.

The new series of Slow Horses will premiere on 16 September, with episodes released weekly until 21 October.
